title: "Audit Analytics in SQL"

::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Reconcile a population to the general ledger in SQL before testing it, and explain why an audit test on an unreconciled population proves little.
2. Trace ledger postings to their source documents and documents to the ledger with anti-joins, combine the tests into one list of exceptions, and test cutoff with document and posting dates.
3. Perform a three-way match of purchase orders, goods receipts, and supplier invoices, summing quantities to the purchase order line and applying a price tolerance.
4. Test approvals across a business process against each approver's limit, role, and employment dates.
5. Test the time, labor, payroll, and payment records behind a cost as one chain, and judge what the exceptions mean for the cost.
6. Organize audit queries into a documented library that can be rerun each period.
:::


## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

You are back on the internal audit team of Chapter 8. The audit committee has read the controller's analysis of the manufacturing variance. The plant paid for about half as many hours again as its standards allowed, more and more of them overtime, while the standards stayed where they were. Before it accepts that explanation, the committee wants to know whether the records behind it can be trusted. Were the hours worked, approved, recorded against the right work, and paid to the right people? The chief audit executive has given you three assignments, all to be done in the database this time.

The first is to confirm that the ledger and its populations can be relied on, by reconciling them and tracing postings to their documents. The second is to test the purchasing chain that supplies the plant, from order to receipt to invoice, and the approvals along it. The third is to test the time, labor, and payroll records behind the variance itself. The chief audit executive also wants the tests saved as a library of queries that the team can rerun every quarter. This chapter shows how to do all three, and how to turn the queries into a library.



## From Samples to Populations

Chapter 8 tested Charles River's payments, receivables, and journal entries in Excel. Each test brought one population into a workbook, reconciled it, and examined every row. SQL does the same work without importing anything, and it removes the limits that a workbook sets on how many tables a test can touch. A test that follows a purchase from its order through its receipt to its invoice, or a labor hour from the time clock through the payroll to the payment, joins five or six tables at once. In a workbook, each of those tables would have to be imported and merged, and a test that reaches across the whole process is exactly the kind that shows whether a control worked.

As Chapter 8 explained, testing an entire population rather than a sample changes what an exception means. A sample finds errors at a rate that the auditor projects to the population, while a population test finds the actual items, each of which needs a disposition. As Chapter 1 noted, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) amended its standards in 2024 to clarify the auditor's responsibilities when using technology-assisted analysis of this kind (PCAOB, 2024). The power of a full-population test also raises the stakes of its inputs. A query that runs against an incomplete table, or that joins on keys that do not match, can report a clean result that means nothing. That is why every test in this chapter begins with a reconciliation.


## Reconciling Before Testing

An audit test is only as complete as the population it runs on. Before testing journal entries, you confirm that the entries in the JournalEntry table add up to the journal entry postings in the ledger. Before testing the payroll behind a cost, you confirm that the payroll registers add up to what the ledger charged. As Chapter 8 noted, the audit data analytics guide of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) includes considerations for assessing the reliability of that data (AICPA, 2026).

In SQL, a reconciliation is usually two aggregate queries, one on the document table and one on the ledger, or a single query that joins their totals. The result should agree to the cent. When it does not, the difference is itself the first finding, and it must be explained before the population is used. In Exercises 6.1 and 10.1, the invoice lines of fiscal 2026 differed from the ledger by three invoices posted in the year after their date. In Chapter 8, the receivables ledger held an opening balance that no invoice supported. Either difference, left unexplained, would have undermined every test built on the population.


## Tracing in Both Directions

The ledger's source-document columns, which Chapter 3 introduced, allow a trace in two directions. From the ledger to the documents, the test asks whether every posting points to a document that exists. An anti-join from GLEntry to the document table on SourceDocumentID finds the postings that point to nothing. From the documents to the ledger, the test asks whether every document was posted. An anti-join from the document table to GLEntry finds the documents with no posting. The first test addresses the existence of what the ledger records, and the second its completeness, as @fig-12-01 shows.

![Tracing in Both Directions Between the Ledger and Its Documents.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-01-two-way-trace.svg){#fig-12-01 fig-alt="The general ledger on the left and the source document tables on the right, linked by SourceDocumentType and SourceDocumentID. An arrow from the ledger to the documents is labeled existence: an anti-join finds postings whose document does not exist. An arrow from the documents to the ledger is labeled completeness: an anti-join finds documents that were never posted. A third test, cutoff, compares each document's date with the posting date of its ledger rows."}

The two directions often need several queries, one for each kind of document. UNION ALL stacks the results of queries with the same columns into one result, so the exceptions of every test can be listed together, each labeled with the test that found it:

```sql
SELECT 'Posting with no payment' AS Test, gl.GLEntryID AS RecordID
FROM GLEntry AS gl
    LEFT JOIN PayrollPayment AS pp
        ON pp.PayrollPaymentID = gl.SourceDocumentID
WHERE gl.SourceDocumentType = 'PayrollPayment'
    AND pp.PayrollPaymentID IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Invoice with no posting', si.SalesInvoiceID
FROM SalesInvoice AS si
    LEFT JOIN GLEntry AS gl ON gl.SourceDocumentType = 'SalesInvoice'
        AND gl.SourceDocumentID = si.SalesInvoiceID
WHERE gl.GLEntryID IS NULL;
```

The queries joined by UNION ALL must return the same number of columns, in the same order, and the column names come from the first query. UNION without ALL also removes duplicate rows, which is rarely what an exceptions list should do.

A third test uses the same columns to test cutoff. A document's own date says when the event happened, and the ledger's PostingDate says when it was recorded. A sales invoice dated in December and posted in January records revenue in the wrong fiscal year. Comparing the two dates, and especially their years, finds the documents recorded in a different period from the one in which they occurred.


{{< include _tutorial-01.qmd >}}


## The Three-Way Match

A purchase leaves three documents: the purchase order that authorized it, the goods receipt that recorded what arrived, and the supplier invoice that billed for it. The three-way match compares them. A supplier should not be paid for more than was ordered and received, or at a price above the one the order approved. Chapter 1 named the three-way match as one of the tests that the Procure-to-Pay tables support (@tbl-01-03), and in SQL it becomes a comparison of totals at the level of the purchase order line.

The level matters. A purchase order line may be received in several deliveries and invoiced on several invoices, so comparing a single receipt with a single invoice line, row by row, reports a mismatch wherever a delivery was split. The comparison must first sum the quantities received and the quantities invoiced for each purchase order line, in derived tables, and then compare the sums with the quantity ordered, as @fig-12-03 shows. A line is fully matched when the three quantities agree. Other outcomes include a line not yet received, a line partly received, and a line received but not yet fully invoiced. A line invoiced above what was received, or received above what was ordered, is an exception.

Prices are compared the same way, with the invoice's unit cost against the order's. Some difference is normal: the purchase price variance of Exercise 9.2 records it. A tolerance, such as two or three percent, separates ordinary differences from exceptions to be investigated. The goods received but not yet invoiced at a year-end are not exceptions either. They are a liability that the company should have accrued, and their total should agree with the ledger account that records it.

![The Three-Way Match at the Level of the Purchase Order Line.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-03-three-way-match.svg){#fig-12-03 fig-alt="A purchase order line from Charles River at the top, with its ordered quantity and unit cost. On the left, its two goods receipt lines are summed into a received quantity; on the right, its three supplier invoice lines are summed into an invoiced quantity, and each invoice price is compared with the order price. The three quantities agree, so the line is matched, although one receipt line was billed on two invoices. Below, a table lists the possible statuses: matched; not yet received; partly received; received but not yet fully invoiced, which is an accrual; and two exceptions, invoiced above received and received above ordered."}


## Testing Approvals Across a Process

An approval control works only if the approver was entitled to approve. SQL tests entitlement by joining each document to the Employee row of its approver and comparing the document with the approver's attributes. An amount above the approver's MaxApprovalAmount is an approval above authority. A document date after the approver's TerminationDate is an approval by someone who no longer worked for the company, and a creator who is also the approver breaks the segregation of duties. An approver whose job title has nothing to do with the process, such as a sales employee approving purchases, is not a violation in itself, but it is worth a question.

These tests look for a small number of exceptions in a large population, and they return a clean result more often than not. A clean result is evidence too, provided the population was reconciled first. An approval test can also reveal concentration, which is not an exception but a risk. When one person approves nearly every document in a process, that person's approval is the whole control, and its failure would go unnoticed.


{{< include _tutorial-02.qmd >}}


## Testing the Records Behind a Cost

The manufacturing variance is built from a chain of records, which @fig-12-06 traces. An employee clocks in and out, and the time clock entry records the hours, with an overtime approval when the overtime is long enough to need one. The hours are recorded against the operation of a work order, or as indirect time. The payroll register pays for the hours, and a payroll payment disburses the net pay. The ledger records the cost and the payment. An auditor tests each link: that the time was approved, that it was recorded against work that was still in progress, that the people paid were employed, that each approved register was paid once, and that each payment was approved before it was made.

![The Chain of Records Behind the Labor Cost.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-06-labor-record-chain.svg){#fig-12-06 fig-alt="A chain of five boxes from left to right: time clock entry, labor time entry, payroll register, payroll payment, and general ledger, each naming the key that links it to the record before it. The last link, a posting to the ledger, is dashed. Beneath each box, the test that checks it: overtime above half an hour has an approval; direct time is recorded on or before its operation ended; the employee was employed on the pay date; each approved register has one payment, made after approval; and every payroll payment posting traces to an existing payment."}

Tests of a chain like this find two kinds of exception. Isolated exceptions, such as a single register paid to a terminated employee, are failures in the operation of a control, and each needs a disposition. Systematic patterns, such as a large share of hours recorded after the operations they belong to were finished, point to the design of a process. They do not necessarily mean that anyone was paid for time not worked, but they mean that the records cannot support some of the conclusions drawn from them. An auditor reports both kinds, and distinguishes them.

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Payroll is a common area for population testing, because the tables are large and the controls are well defined. The typical frauds also leave traces in the data: employees paid after they have left, hours that exceed what was clocked, overtime without approval, and payments made to the same bank account for different employees. Tests like these are often run every pay period, so that an exception is found while it can still be corrected, rather than at the year-end audit.
:::


{{< include _tutorial-03.qmd >}}


## Chapter 8's Tests in SQL

The tests you ran in Excel in Chapter 8 translate directly into SQL, and in SQL they can join tables that the workbook kept apart. A duplicate payment test groups the payments by supplier and invoice number, or by supplier and check number, and keeps the groups with more than one row. A near-duplicate test joins the payments to themselves, a self-join, matching the same supplier and amount on different dates within a window of days:

```sql
SELECT a.PaymentNumber, b.PaymentNumber AS MatchNumber,
    a.SupplierID, a.Amount, a.PaymentDate, b.PaymentDate AS MatchDate
FROM DisbursementPayment AS a
    INNER JOIN DisbursementPayment AS b
        ON b.SupplierID = a.SupplierID AND b.Amount = a.Amount
            AND b.DisbursementID > a.DisbursementID
WHERE a.PaymentDate <> b.PaymentDate
    AND julianday(b.PaymentDate) - julianday(a.PaymentDate)
        BETWEEN -30 AND 30
    AND a.PaymentDate <= '2026-12-31' AND b.PaymentDate <= '2026-12-31';
```

The condition `b.DisbursementID > a.DisbursementID` keeps each pair once, instead of twice in opposite orders. A sequence test uses LAG, partitioned by year, to compare each document number with the one before it and report any step greater than one. A first-digit test needs the first significant digit of each amount. `printf('%e', Amount)` writes an amount in scientific notation, as 6.884200e+02 for 688.42, so its first character is the first significant digit even for amounts below one dollar. `LOG10(1 + 1.0 / Digit)` gives the Benford expectation for each digit. Grouped and compared, they produce the same mean absolute deviation as the workbook of Tutorial 8.1. The exercises at the end of the chapter build these tests.


## A Library of Audit Queries

A test that is saved, documented, and run again every period becomes part of the company's control environment. An audit query library is a set of such tests, usually one script for each area, with a consistent structure. Each test states its objective, the population it runs on and the reconciliation that proves the population complete, the query, the expected result, and the disposition of any exception. @tbl-12-01 shows the library that this chapter builds.

| Area | Test | Technique |
|---|---|---|
| Ledger | Journal entry population reconciliation | Aggregates on two tables |
| Ledger | Postings with no document; documents with no posting | Anti-joins, UNION ALL |
| Ledger | Cutoff: posting year against document year | Join, date comparison |
| Purchasing | Three-way match by purchase order line | Derived tables, CASE |
| Purchasing | Goods received not invoiced against the ledger | Left join, aggregates |
| Purchasing | Approvals above limit, by terminated employees, and self-approved | Join to Employee |
| Labor and payroll | Overtime above the threshold without approval | Join, CASE |
| Labor and payroll | Labor recorded after the operation ended | Join, date comparison |
| Labor and payroll | Registers paid to terminated employees, unpaid, or paid before approval | Joins, anti-join |

: The audit query library of this chapter {#tbl-12-01}

@fig-12-08 shows the start of such a script, Audit.sql, as the tutorials of this chapter leave it. Views make the library easy to rerun: each test can be saved as a view, and a summary query can count the exceptions of every view in one result.

![The Start of an Audit Query Library.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-08-audit-library.svg){#fig-12-08 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor holding the script Audit.sql. A header comment names the engagement, the database, the preparer and reviewer, and the date. Below it, each test is a section that begins with a comment giving its number, its objective, its population and reconciliation, and its expected result, followed by the query. The first sections shown are the journal entry reconciliation and the combined trace of postings and documents."}

Whatever the form, the library itself needs the controls it tests. Changes to a test should be reviewed and recorded, and each run's results should be kept as a workpaper, with the date, the data it ran on, and the reviewer. A library that anyone can change without a record would undermine the evidence it produces.


## Looking Ahead

This chapter has applied SQL to the work of an internal auditor. You reconciled populations to the ledger before testing them, traced postings to their documents and documents to their postings, combined the exceptions into one list with UNION ALL, and tested cutoff with dates. You performed a three-way match at the level of the purchase order line, reconciled the goods received but not invoiced to the ledger, and tested approvals against the approvers' limits, roles, and employment dates. You tested the chain of time, labor, payroll, and payment records behind the manufacturing variance, and you translated the tests of Chapter 8 into queries for a reusable library.

The audit also answers the committee's question. The ledger and its populations reconcile, and the purchasing chain matches. The payroll behind the variance ties to the ledger to the cent, and its exceptions are few, specific, and isolated. The extra hours were clocked, approved where the policy requires it, and paid, so the variance is a real cost, not an artifact of false records. That also answers the question the controller asked at the start of Chapter 9: the variance grew because the plant used more paid hours for the same output, while the standards stayed where they were. Whether to bring the hours down or to revise the standards is now a decision for management. The audit also found a systematic pattern. A growing share of direct labor was recorded against operations that had already finished, most of it at Packing. That pattern does not change the cost, but it means the operation-level records cannot say where in the plant the extra hours were spent, and the controller's next analysis should not rely on them until the recording is fixed.

This chapter completes Part III. SQL has let you ask questions of whole tables at once, from the first SELECT to a library of audit tests. Part IV turns from finding answers to communicating them, with reports and dashboards that let managers and audit committees explore the evidence for themselves.
